docs.title: Limpopo Digital Twin Portal
docs.text:
Documentation for the TerriaJS portal showcasing the Digital Twin (DT) of the Limpopo River Basin, developed for the International Water Management Institute (IWMI).

About this documentation

This is the v2 guide — it documents the portal now running at limpopo.digitaltwins.iwmi.org (TerriaMap 0.4.1 / TerriaJS 8.9.5, built 2026-05-15). The screenshots are captured from that release. For the original 2024 portal, choose v1 in the version selector in the header.

Open the portal

Launch the live portal at limpopo.digitaltwins.iwmi.org. See Release Notes for what changed since the 2024 release — a redesigned interface, five new catalogue categories, and new tools including an AI chatbot and a SWAT extraction tool.

docs.title: What the portal does
docs.text:
The WebGIS Portal (Phase 2) is an advanced geospatial web portal that visualises and lets you interact with spatial datasets relevant to the Limpopo River basin. It features a Digital Twin of the basin, aggregating and interpolating data from satellite imagery, in-situ sensors and numerical model outputs.

Phase 2 builds on the foundation established in Phase 1, using the TerriaJS framework — an open-source platform for web-based geospatial catalogue exploration. The portal draws inspiration from platforms such as Digital Earth Africa (DE Africa) and NationalMap.

Figure 1: The Limpopo Digital Twin portal — the basin on the 3D globe, with the workbench and data controls on the left.

docs.title: Key capabilities at a glance
docs.text:
Capability What it gives you Geospatial visualisation Interactive 2D and 3D views of basin data Thematic data catalogue Curated datasets across eleven thematic categories Time series analysis Explore change over time with a timeline slider Workbench Toggle, restyle, reorder and compare active layers My Data Add local files or web services without uploading them Stories Capture scenes into a narrative you can share Share & print Shareable URLs, PNG export and printable views AI chatbot (Water Copilot) Ask questions about the basin and get guided answers SWAT Extraction Tool Query modelled flows for a channel over a date range

New in v2

Compared with the 2024 release, v2 adds five catalogue categories (Flood Monitoring & Early Warning, Drought Monitoring & Risk Assessment, Citizen Science, Water Use Monitoring and Analysis, and Data Sources & Providers), two new tools (the Water Copilot chatbot and the SWAT Extraction Tool), an expanded basemap set, and a redesigned workbench. Signing in is now required to open the portal.

docs.title: Conclusion of the source report
docs.text: The WebGIS Portal represents a significant advancement in geospatial data visualisation for IWMI. Built on the robust TerriaJS framework, it integrates diverse datasets and provides an intuitive interface for exploring the Limpopo River basin — supporting informed decision-making in water resource management across the basin.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: For help with the portal, or for questions about the datasets it publishes, contact the IWMI geospatial team at iwmigeospatial@gmail.com, or use the Feedback form built into the portal.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
This guide walks through the Limpopo WebGIS Portal interface, feature by feature, in roughly the order you meet them.

Page Covers Getting Started The homepage, location search and opening the map Data Catalogue Browsing, searching, previewing and adding datasets Dataset Themes What each of the five thematic categories contains My Data Adding your own local files and web services Workbench Managing the layers currently on the map Map Tools View controls, compare, pedestrian mode, measuring, settings Stories & Sharing Building narratives and sharing or printing the map Help & Support Tours, guides, related maps, feedback and version info Water Copilot Opening the AI assistant, what it can answer and how to ask

Two ways to learn the interface

The portal ships with a built-in guided Take the Tour walkthrough and a Getting Started with the Map video. Both are reachable from the Help feature at any time — you do not have to leave the map to use them.

Click Explore data in the workbench (or Explore map data on the welcome panel) to open the Data Catalogue. In v2 this is a two-pane panel: the category tree on the left, and a dataset preview on the right.

Figure 3: The Data Catalogue. The left pane lists the eleven thematic categories; selecting a dataset previews it on the right.

At the top of the panel are two tabs — Data (the curated catalogue) and My Data (your own files, see My Data) — a Search the catalogue box, and a Done button that returns you to the map.

docs.title: The eleven categories
docs.text:
v2 expands the catalogue from five thematic categories to eleven. Five are new since the 2024 release (marked New):

Category Contents Natural Basin Characteristic Physiography, land cover and land use, 3D point clouds, climate Flood Monitoring & Early Warning New — flood monitoring and early-warning layers Drought Monitoring & Risk Assessment New — drought monitoring and risk layers Socio-Economic Profile Population and demographic data Water Resources Surface water sources and infrastructure Citizen Science New — community-contributed observations (e.g. miniSASS, FishTRAC) Water Use Monitoring and Analysis New — water accounting and use monitoring Ecosystems E-flow regions, monitoring, alerts and warnings Satellite Images GeoMAD (Sentinel-2), Water Observations from Space Data Sources & Providers New — provenance and provider information for the catalogue

See Dataset Themes for a walkthrough of what each category contains.

docs.title: Searching the catalogue
docs.text: Use Search the catalogue to find a dataset by name across all categories — faster than walking the tree.

docs.title: Previewing and adding data
docs.text:
Click a category to expand it, then select a dataset. Its preview appears in the right-hand pane with a description and an add control (the + icon). Typical preview information includes:

  1. Dataset description — what the data is and why it matters.
  2. Add to the map — draws the dataset on the globe (the + icon; hold Shift and click + to add several datasets at once).
  3. Service contact — who to contact about the dataset.
  4. GetCapabilities URL — for integrating the dataset into other GIS software.
  5. DOI and data source — citation identifier and primary provider.

Add several at once

The catalogue prompts "Press Shift and click + to add multiple datasets." Use Go to the map or Done when you have finished selecting.

Once added, a dataset appears in the Workbench, where you can toggle it, change its opacity, restyle it, chart it and compare it.

docs.title: Feature information
docs.text: Clicking a feature on the map opens its Feature Information — the attributes behind that point, with options to download the underlying table (CSV or JSON) and to show the raw data. For datasets with a temporal dimension, a chart and a timeline let you explore change over a chosen date range.

The Data Catalogue groups data into eleven thematic categories in v2. This page describes what each one holds. The mechanics of previewing, adding, styling and charting any dataset are the same throughout — see Data Catalogue.

Figure 4: The eleven thematic categories in the v2 Data Catalogue.

docs.title: Natural Basin Characteristic
docs.text:
The physical setting of the basin. Sub-collections include:

  • Physiography — elevation and topography, basin and sub-basin boundaries, the channel network.
  • 3D point clouds — high-resolution drone-surveyed elevation for the Oliphants River and the Crocodile River System (Upper and Lower).
  • Land cover and land use — Land Use, Irrigated Mapping and the Vegetation Condition Index (VCI); several are available as time series.
  • Climate — CHIRPS historical rainfall, rainfall monitoring and forecast, and rainfall anomaly charts.

docs.title: Flood Monitoring & Early Warning
docs.text:
New in v2

Layers for monitoring flooding across the basin and supporting early-warning — observed and forecast flood extent and related indicators.

docs.title: Drought Monitoring & Risk Assessment
docs.text:
New in v2

Drought monitoring and risk layers, complementing the climate and vegetation datasets for assessing drought onset, severity and exposure.

docs.title: Socio-Economic Profile
docs.text: Socio-economic conditions within the basin, including population and demographic factors. Population data can be styled from the display dropdown — by sub-basin, area, polygon ID or population.

docs.title: Water Resources
docs.text:
The availability, distribution and use of water resources:

  • Surface Water Sources — including discharge monitoring from the SWAT model (present-day, gauging stations and forecast).
  • Infrastructure — including dam locations.

docs.title: Citizen Science
docs.text:
New in v2

Community-contributed observations of river and ecosystem health — for example miniSASS (river biomonitoring) and FishTRAC. These bring ground observations alongside the modelled and remotely-sensed layers.

docs.title: Water Use Monitoring and Analysis
docs.text:
New in v2

Water accounting and water-use monitoring layers — how much water is available and how it is being used across the basin.

docs.title: Ecosystems
docs.text:
Datasets on the basin's ecosystems and environmental flows:

Dataset Contents E-flow Regions Ecological flow regions E-flow Monitoring and Forecasting Current and forecast ecological flows E-flow Alert Levels Levels of ecological flow alert SWAT Incremental Contributions Incremental contributions from the SWAT model E-flow Warnings Alerts on ecological flow conditions

E-flow charts expose attributes such as Availability Surplus, Deficit, SWAT Present Flow and E-Flow; hover a point on the curve to read its values.

docs.title: Satellite Images
docs.text: Imagery for remote sensing and environmental monitoring, including Rolling Monthly GeoMAD (Sentinel-2) and the Water Observations from Space all-time summary.

docs.title: Data Sources & Providers
docs.text:
New in v2

Provenance for the catalogue — who supplies each dataset and where it comes from — gathered into one category so you can trace a layer back to its source.

Not sure where to start? Open the Data Catalogue, expand a category, and select a dataset to preview it before adding it to the map.

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text:
The v2 portal is access-controlled: opening limpopo.digitaltwins.iwmi.org takes you to the Digital Twin Applications Single Sign-On page before the map loads. You can sign in in three ways:

  • Email and password — enter your credentials and click Sign In (tick Remember me to stay signed in; use Forgot Password? to reset).
  • Sign in with Google — use your Google account.
  • Sign in with Microsoft — use your Microsoft account.

New users can Register from the link at the bottom of the sign-in page.

Once signed in, the top bar shows Account and Log out; use Account to manage your profile.

Need access?

If you cannot sign in or register, contact the IWMI geospatial team at iwmigeospatial@gmail.com.

docs.title: The welcome screen
docs.text:
On first load the portal shows a "Let's get you started" welcome panel over the map.

Figure 1: The “Let's get you started” welcome panel.

It offers three ways in:

  • Take the tour — an interactive walkthrough that names each control on screen.
  • I'll need some help — opens the help guide.
  • Explore map data — dismisses the welcome panel and opens the Data Catalogue straight away.

Dismiss the panel with Close message and don't show me this again (or the ✕) to go directly to the map. A short coach-mark then points at Help in the top bar — click Got it, thanks! to clear it.

First visit? Take the tour

The tour labels every control, which makes the rest of this guide much easier to follow.

docs.title: The main interface
docs.text:
Figure 2: The main interface — workbench and data controls on the left, the 3D globe centre, map tools down the right, and the account and tool bar across the top.

The interface has four regions:

  • Workbench (left) — the IWMI / LIMCOM / CGIAR Digital Transformation logo, a location search, the Explore data and Upload data buttons, and the list of datasets currently on the map. See Workbench.
  • Map (centre) — the Cesium 3D globe, showing the basin outline over satellite imagery.
  • Map tools (right) — orientation, zoom, location, compare, pedestrian mode and measuring. See Map Tools.
  • Top bar — About, Account, Log out on the left; Map Settings, Help, Story and Share / Print on the right.

docs.title: Search for a location
docs.text: The Search for locations bar at the top of the workbench jumps to a place within the Limpopo River basin. The search is geocoded and scoped to the basin study area.

docs.title: Explore map data
docs.text: Click Explore data (or Explore map data on the welcome panel) to open the Data Catalogue. You can add several datasets at once; each is then managed from the Workbench.

docs.title: Interactive map controls
docs.text:
The core navigation controls behave like any web map:

  • Zoom and pan — navigate the datasets intuitively.
  • Basemaps — choose a background map in Map Settings (the v2 set includes Bing, OpenStreetMap, Esri, Dark Matter, Positron and more).
  • 2D / 3D — switch between the 3D globe, a smooth 3D view, and a flat 2D map in Map Settings.
  • Time series — explore temporal change with the timeline, where a dataset provides it.

docs.title: Accessibility and compatibility
docs.text:
• Cross-browser — works across all major browsers.
  • Responsive — adapts to tablets and smaller screens.

docs.title: Map Settings
docs.text:
Map Settings (top bar) customises how the map is drawn.

Figure 7: Map Settings — view mode, terrain, basemaps, timeline and quality.
  • Map View — 3D Terrain, 3D Smooth or 2D.
  • Show Terrain on the — Left / Both / Right, with an option so terrain hides underground features.
  • Base Map — v2 offers a wider set than the 2024 release: Bing Aerial with Labels (default), Bing Aerial, Bing Roads, OpenStreetMap, OpenTopoMap, Esri World Imagery, Esri Topographic, Dark Matter, Positron (Light) and Natural Earth II.
  • Timeline → Always show — keeps the time-series controls on screen.
  • Image Optimisation — use native device resolution.
  • Map Quality — a Quality ↔ Performance slider.

docs.title: View controls
docs.text:
The Change view control (the ring-and-cross icon) rotates the map through 360°, and a double-click resets it. Beneath it:

Control Action Home Returns to the default globe view + / – Zoom in / out (the mouse wheel also zooms) Location Live location tracking — click Allow in the popup Pan Drag the map with the left mouse button

docs.title: Compare
docs.text:
The Compare tool (Enable side-by-side comparison between two different sets of data) puts two datasets side by side in split-screen mode.

Figure 8: Side-by-side comparison mode.
  1. Click Compare to enter split-screen mode.
  2. Choose the two datasets to compare.
  3. Drag the split bar to align them; assign each dataset to Left, Right or Both.

Terrain note

Terrain layers can obscure underground features — relevant depending on the datasets being compared.

docs.title: Pedestrian mode
docs.text:
Pedestrian Mode gives a street-level view for detailed exploration.

Figure 9: Pedestrian Mode — a ground-level view of the data.

Use the control tool to rotate the view; Space moves forward and Shift moves backward.

docs.title: Measure
docs.text:
The Line Measure tool (Measure distance between locations) measures the distance between two or more points on the map.

Figure 10: Measuring distance between points.

docs.title: Water Copilot chatbot
docs.text:
New in v2

Open Chatbot (bottom-right of the map) launches Water Copilot, an AI assistant. Ask questions about the basin and its data in plain language and get guided answers and navigation help. The assistant opens in a panel beside the map. See Water Copilot for what it can answer and how to ask.

docs.title: SWAT Extraction Tool
docs.text:
New in v2

The SWAT Extraction Tool queries modelled flows from the SWAT hydrological model for a specific river channel.

Figure 11: The SWAT Extraction Tool — choose a flow type, channel and date range, then fetch data. Tabs switch between Map, Table, Help and ProbFlo.
  • Select Flow Type — e.g. Natural Flows.
  • Channel ID — the channel to query.
  • Start Date / End Date — the period of interest.
  • Condition — a filter on the flow condition.
  • FETCH DATA — retrieves the modelled series; the MAP / TABLE / HELP / PROBFLO tabs switch between the map picker, the results table, help, and the ProbFlo view.

The Give Feedback tool sends comments or questions directly to the developers.

Figure 12: The feedback form — name and email are optional; you can include your current map view.

docs.text: Along the bottom of the map are data attribution, the basemap selector, and the disclaimers that apply to the data in use, plus a live Lat / Lon / Elev readout and a scale bar.

The My Data feature lets you bring your own datasets onto the map for localised analysis. In v2 it is the second tab of the Data Catalogue: click Upload data in the workbench (or Explore data, then the My Data tab).

Figure 5: The My Data tab — drag and drop a file, or use Add Local Data / Add Web Data.

Your data stays on your machine

Data added through My Data is not saved or uploaded to the internet — the panel says so explicitly. It is rendered locally in your browser, so sensitive information stays private.

docs.title: Adding local data
docs.text:
Drag a file into the area marked "Drag and drop a file here to view it locally on the map", or click Add Local Data and choose a file. Supported formats:

  • GeoTIFF
  • Shapefiles
  • KML / KMZ
  • GeoJSON
  • CSV with location coordinates

The platform renders the data immediately, ready to view and interact with. Use the Workbench tools to toggle visibility, adjust opacity and compare your dataset against other layers.

docs.title: Adding web data
docs.text:
Click Add Web Data to pull in a dataset from an external service. This accepts URLs from WMS (Web Map Service), WFS (Web Feature Service) and other compatible online geospatial sources.

  1. Click Add Web Data.
  2. Paste the service or data-source URL.
  3. The platform fetches the data and draws it on the map.

Finding a service URL

Catalogue datasets expose a GetCapabilities URL in their preview — that is the style of URL Add Web Data expects from external services.

docs.text: Benefit What it means Flexibility Visualise your datasets without uploading or storing them on the platform Privacy Data is not uploaded or saved to the internet, so sensitive information stays secure Integration Combine your own data with the platform's catalogue for richer analysis

docs.title: The Story feature
docs.text:
The Story feature (top bar) builds shareable narratives by capturing map scenes with explanatory text — combining the visual and interactive strengths of the map with a guided storyline.

Figure 13: The Story builder.
  • Story Editor — the interface for creating and managing stories, integrating maps, data layers and narrative text.
  • Capture Scene — saves the current map view, with a title and description, as a step in the story.
  • Getting Started — links to a Terria video on building data stories.

Add scenes in the order you want to present them, then share the finished story using Share / Print.

docs.title: Share / Print
docs.text:
The Share / Print feature (top bar) shares or exports the current map.

Figure 14: Share / Print — a shareable URL, PNG download and print view.
  • Share URL — generates a link that reproduces your current map ("Anyone with this URL will be able to access this map"); the URL is shortened automatically. Click Copy.
  • Download map (png) — saves the current view as a PNG image.
  • Show Print View — opens a printable version of the map.
  • Advanced options — expand for extra settings, including whether to include your story in the shared content.

Older share links

Share links created by older versions of TerriaJS can be migrated — see the Share & Story Migration guide in the Help feature.

docs.title: Water Copilot
docs.text:
Water Copilot is the portal's AI assistant. You ask a question about the Limpopo basin in plain language, and it answers by running the Digital Twin's own data services: rainfall records, environmental-flow monitoring, reservoir storage, flood stations, water accounting, satellite products and the project's document library. Answers come back as text, charts, tables and download links, inside a panel beside the map.

It is a different way into the same data the catalogue holds. Where the catalogue asks you to find a dataset and add it as a layer, the assistant lets you ask for the number, chart or comparison you actually want.

Figure 17: Water Copilot opens bottom-right, with an expand button, a language switch and a sign-in prompt.

docs.title: Opening the assistant
docs.text:
Click the round chatbot icon at the bottom-right of the map (its tooltip reads Open Chatbot). A panel opens over the corner of the map.

  • The expand button (⛶) at the top of the panel switches to full screen; click it again to return to the corner. The × closes the panel.
  • The language switch (flag and EN) at the top of the panel toggles the assistant between English and Portuguese.
  • The assistant asks you to Sign In the first time. Use the same IWMI Digital Twins account you signed into the portal with. First-time users can Register from the same screen.

The panel is separate from the map

Charts, maps and files the assistant produces appear inside the panel as images and links. They are not added to the map as layers. To put data on the map, use the Data Catalogue; to analyse a drawn area on the map, use the analysis tools in the Water Use Monitoring and Analysis group.

docs.title: What you can ask
docs.text:
The assistant answers only from the Digital Twin's data services, so its scope is the scope of those services. Broadly:

Topic What it can do Example question Rainfall Find stations near a place, return historical and forecast series with a chart Show rainfall near Tzaneen for the last six months. Environmental flows Current values and alert status at e-flow sites, compliance charts, site details Which e-flow sites are in alert this month? Reservoirs and drought Find a dam by name, storage status, storage and seasonal charts, a basin-wide storage overview How full is Massingir dam, and how does this year compare? Floods Flood stations, current severity ranking, past flood events, hydrographs and return periods, flood animations Where is flooding happening right now in the basin? Water accounting Basin overview, water balance by year, evapotranspiration fractions, per-capita availability, basin closure, environmental stress, monthly maps Give me a comprehensive water accounting analysis of the basin. Water use Monthly water consumption of irrigated areas around a place How much water did irrigated farms near Hoedspruit use last year? River health MiniSASS citizen-science sites, scores, trends and dashboards Which rivers have the best MiniSASS scores? Satellite products List Open Data Cube products, their dates and bands, and render a map image Show me the latest irrigated-area map for the lower basin. Hydrological model Monthly simulated channel flows from the SWAT model, present and natural, 2001 to 2025 Compare present and natural flow for channel cha0125 in 2020. Documents Search the basin literature library and the Digital Twin's own reports and publications What do the reports say about groundwater in the Limpopo? Gauge plates Read a water level from a photograph of a gauge plate Attach the photo and give the station.

In development

Field-scale tools that sharpen WaPOR evapotranspiration from 300 m to 20 m, the same ones available in the catalogue's Water Use Monitoring and Analysis group, are being connected to the assistant. Until they are, ask for them on the map rather than in the chat.

docs.title: How it answers
docs.text:
A few habits are built in, and knowing them makes the assistant easier to work with.

  • It looks the answer up rather than recalling it. For any factual or numerical question it runs the data services and reports what they return. If there is no data for what you asked, it says so and suggests an alternative: a different period, a nearby station, a coarser aggregation.
  • Charts are shown inline, data is downloadable. Where a service produces a chart it appears in the reply, and where it produces a file you get a Download CSV link.
  • Every analysis ends with a summary, key insights and an interpretation, with units and the period covered stated.
  • It asks before it assumes. Dates, stations, dams and channels are yours to choose, so when a question leaves one open the assistant offers the options and waits, rather than picking for you.
  • Copy on any reply copies the text, or the image, for use elsewhere.

docs.title: Asking good questions
docs.text:
• Name the place. A town, river, dam or scheme is enough. If the assistant asks for coordinates instead, give a nearby town, or latitude and longitude in decimal degrees.
  • Give the period. Dates in YYYY-MM-DD work best. For monthly products, YYYY-MM is fine.
  • Say "comprehensive" when you want the full water accounting picture; the assistant then runs the whole set of accounting analyses rather than one.
  • Ask for the CSV when you want to take the numbers away.
  • Know which data is live. E-flow values and alerts, rainfall, flood monitoring and reservoir status are near real time. Satellite products, SWAT model outputs and documents are not, and the assistant will tell you the period it used.
  • Be specific with the model. SWAT channels are numbered cha0002 to cha1436; use the channel code, not the river name.

docs.title: Conversations, feedback and account
docs.text: Your conversations are saved to your account, so you can pick an earlier one up again. Each reply carries a thumbs up and thumbs down; use them, with a comment if you like, since the ratings go to the team that maintains the assistant and shape what it gets better at. Your portal account details are under Account in the top bar (see Help & Support).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The assistant is only as good as the data behind it. Check the period, the units and the station or site it used before you act on a figure, especially where it has told you the data was incomplete.
  • Evapotranspiration-based water use is water consumed by crops and soil, not water abstracted from a river or canal. Abstraction will be higher.
  • Large requests, many months or many stations at once, take longer and may be trimmed. Ask in smaller pieces if a reply seems cut short.
  • It does not add layers to the map, edit your workbench, or change portal settings.

docs.title: Managing the whole list

Above the dataset list, three actions apply to everything at once:

Control Effect Disable All Hides every dataset without removing it Collapse All Minimises every dataset card for a cleaner view Remove All Clears every dataset from the workbench

docs.title: Per-dataset controls
docs.text:
Each dataset card gives you:

  • Toggle — the switch at the top of the card turns the dataset on or off.
  • Ideal Zoom — moves the map to the view that best frames the dataset.
  • About Data — returns to the catalogue entry and its full description.
  • Three-dot menu (⋮) — Show more actions, opening:

docs.title: Project Overview
docs.text: The WebGIS Portal delivers a comprehensive and user-friendly interface for visualising climatic and water resource datasets. It aggregates and interpolates data from multiple sources — satellite imagery, in-situ sensor data and numerical model outputs — stored primarily on AWS.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The WebGIS Portal Phase 2 project, developed for the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), provides an advanced geospatial web portal for visualising and interacting with spatial datasets relevant to the Limpopo River basin. The platform features a Digital Twin (DT) of the basin.

Phase 2 builds on the foundation established in Phase 1, leveraging the TerriaJS framework — an open-source platform known for web-based geospatial catalogue exploration. The portal draws inspiration from platforms such as Digital Earth Africa (DE Africa) and incorporates improvements based on Phase 1 feedback.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Objective Description Geospatial visualisation Develop a web application forming the foundation of the Digital Twin, to visualise and interact with spatial data specific to the Limpopo River basin Mapping functionalities Implement essential mapping features such as zoom, pan and layer control Data integration Integrate diverse geospatial data sources for accurate, up-to-date information User experience Offer a user-friendly interface for seamless navigation and data exploration Cross-browser compatibility Ensure the portal works effectively across different browsers and devices

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The portal encompasses the following key components:

  • Responsive portal — an interactive WebGIS portal designed for diverse devices.
  • Geospatial data integration — aggregated data from APIs and other sources.
  • Advanced visualisation — tools for visualising data related to irrigated areas.
  • AI-driven chatbot — a chatbot to assist users with queries and navigation.
  • Enhanced time series maps — fixed and enhanced time series maps for better data analysis.
  • Additional shapefiles — inclusion of additional shapefiles for comprehensive data coverage.
  • AWS deployment — hosting on AWS for high availability and scalability.

The WebGIS Portal is built on the TerriaJS framework, chosen for its ability to assemble spatial data catalogues through a mix of manual curation and live querying of online services. docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Terms and acronyms used across this documentation.

docs.title: Platform and project
docs.text: Digital Twin (DT) A virtual representation of the Limpopo River basin, assembled from satellite   imagery, in-situ sensor data and numerical model outputs. TerriaJS The open-source geospatial framework the portal is built on. It assembles   spatial data catalogues through manual curation and live querying of online   services. IWMI International Water Management Institute — the organisation the portal was   developed for. DE Africa Digital Earth Africa, one of the platforms that inspired the portal's design. NationalMap Australia's national map platform, also built on TerriaJS. Cesium ion The platform component providing 3D mapping, data attribution and base map   selection.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text: Workbench The left-hand panel listing every dataset currently active on the map, with   controls for visibility, opacity, styling and removal.   See Workbench. Data Catalogue The thematic collection of curated datasets available to add to the map.   See Data Catalogue. My Data The section for adding your own local files or web services, without   uploading them to the platform. See My Data. Story / Story Editor The narrative tool for capturing map scenes with accompanying text.   See Stories & Sharing. Capture Scene The action that saves the current map view, title and description as a step   in a story. Split Screen Mode The compare view that places two datasets side by side.   See Compare feature. Pedestrian Mode A street-level, ground-based view of the map data. Ideal Zoom A per-dataset option that moves the map to the view best framing that   dataset. Feature Information The panel reporting the underlying attributes of a clicked map feature, with   CSV and JSON export.

docs.title: Data and services
docs.text: WMS Web Map Service — a standard for serving georeferenced map images, accepted   by Add Web Data. WFS Web Feature Service — a standard for serving map feature geometry and   attributes, accepted by Add Web Data. GetCapabilities URL The service URL exposed in a dataset preview, used to integrate the dataset   into other GIS software. GeoTIFF A raster image format carrying embedded georeferencing; supported by   My Data. GeoJSON A JSON-based format for encoding geographic features; supported by My Data. KML / KMZ Keyhole Markup Language (and its zipped form) for geographic annotation;   supported by My Data. Shapefile A widely used vector data format; supported by My Data. DOI Digital Object Identifier — the persistent citation identifier given in a   dataset's preview panel.

docs.title: Hydrology and environment
docs.text: SWAT Soil and Water Assessment Tool — the hydrological model providing present-day   flow and incremental contribution datasets. E-flow Environmental flow — the water regime needed to sustain the basin's   ecosystems. The portal publishes E-flow regions, monitoring and forecasting,   alert levels and warnings. Availability Surplus In the E-flow chart, the amount or unit of surplus available. Deficit In the E-flow chart, the shortfall or lack of data. CHIRPS Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station data — the source   of the historical rainfall dataset. VCI Vegetation Condition Index — a land-cover dataset available as a time series. GeoMAD The geomedian and median absolute deviation product, published here as   Rolling Monthly GeoMAD (Sentinel-2). Sentinel-2 The satellite mission behind the portal's rolling monthly imagery. Water Observations from Space An all-time summary satellite dataset of observed surface water. 3D Point Cloud High-resolution drone-collected elevation data, available for the Oliphants   River and the Crocodile River System (Upper and Lower). Water Copilot The portal's AI assistant, opened from the chatbot icon at the bottom right   of the map. It answers questions about the basin by running the Digital   Twin's data services and returns charts, tables and download links. See   Water Copilot. Evapotranspiration (ET) Water returned to the atmosphere from soil evaporation and plant   transpiration together. In an irrigated area it is the closest satellite   measure of water actually consumed by crops, and is not the same as water   abstracted from a river or canal. WaPOR FAO's Water Productivity Open-access Portal, a satellite-based dataset of   evapotranspiration and related variables for Africa, published every dekad   at 300 m (Level 1) and 100 m (Level 2), with 20 m (Level 3) at selected   irrigation sites. Dekad A ten-day period. WaPOR publishes three per month, starting on the 1<sup>st</sup>, 11<sup>th</sup>   and 21<sup>st</sup>; the third runs to the end of the month.

docs.title: The question
docs.text:
An agricultural extension officer, a water utility or a basin committee wants to know whether a drought is developing, how severe it is compared with past years, which sectors are at risk, and what the coming season looks like.

Drought builds in stages, and the catalogue is organised the same way: meteorological (rain), then soil and vegetation stress, then hydrological (rivers and groundwater), then sectoral risk.

Who Decision Cadence Extension services and farmer organisations Planting advice, drought-tolerant seed, livestock destocking Monthly through the season Water utilities and municipalities Restrictions, borehole rotation, tanker planning Monthly; weekly in a declared drought Basin committees / LIMCOM Declare drought status, trigger cross-border allocation rules Seasonal (Oct, Jan, Apr) Food-security and humanitarian analysts (IPC, WFP) Target assistance by district Seasonal

At a glance — indicator thresholds used in the portal

  • VCI < 35 — vegetation in potential drought stress; crop-failure risk (from the Vegetation Condition Index description).
  • SPI / SPEI < −1 — moderate drought; < −1.5 severe; < −2 extreme.
  • Annual rainfall < 75 % of the long-term mean — a failed year. At the Ingwizi station (upper Shashe) the mean is 606 mm; 2002 recorded 271 mm.
  • E-flow Alert Level 3–5 — the river has crossed into hydrological drought (see Environmental flows).

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. Start with vegetation — the most visible signal. Explore data → search VCI → add The Vegetation Condition Index (VCI). Use the timeline to compare this month with the same month in previous years; VCI is already normalised against history, so low values mean worse than usual, not just dry season. Values below 35 over cropland are the trigger.
  2. Confirm with NDVI Anomaly (DEA) (add it, use Compare against VCI). Agreement between two independent vegetation products is a robust drought signal; disagreement usually means harvest, fire or clearing.
  3. Check the cause — rainfall. Add CHIRPS Historical Rainfall and step the timeline back through the season; add Rainfall Anomalies and click a station circle for its chart (Figure 1). Then add Drought Hazard – SPEI 3-month for the standardised deficit.
  4. Check the soil. Add SMAP Root Zone Soil Moisture (L4, Daily). Root-zone deficit, not just surface dryness, is what limits crops; surface moisture recovers with one shower, root-zone moisture does not.
  5. Check the rivers. Add Eflow Warnings and Eflow Alert Levels, then E-flow Monitoring and Forecasting and click a site for its chart. Rivers below environmental-flow levels mark the transition to hydrological drought (see Environmental flows).
  6. Check storage. Add Dams & Reservoirs Basin Level Estimates: dams marked Low or Critical (Middle Letaba was at 10.5 % in July 2026) show where supply is already constrained (see Reservoir monitoring).
  7. Translate to risk. Add Drought Risk – Agriculture (3-month) and Drought Risk – Water Sector (3-month) with Population underneath to see where stressed conditions meet people.
  8. Look ahead. Add Limpopo Rainfall Anomaly Forecast and the Seasonal Forecast Anomaly (7-month): a dry outlook on top of an existing deficit is the trigger for early action.
  9. Save the sequence as a Story — one scene per stage makes a compelling briefing.

docs.title: Reading the charts
docs.text:
The figures below are the portal's own charts, captured from the Feature Information panel (click a feature) and from the Charts dock that opens with the panel's Expand button. Every station, dam and site chart in the portal follows the same pattern: a summary card, a preview chart, Expand to enlarge, Download for the CSV.

Figure 1: Rainfall Anomalies card for channel cha0036 (Ingwizi, upper Shashe): the current month's observed total, the climatological mean, the anomaly in mm and %, its class, plus the last 7 days and 7-day forecast, with the monthly preview chart.
  • Beware percentage anomalies in the dry season: 0.4 mm observed against a 0.1 mm mean reads +300 %, Very wet — meaningless in August. Judge the class in the wet-season months (Nov–Mar), or read the mm anomaly.
  • The preview chart shows monthly totals since 2001; the shape of each summer peak (tall and narrow, or low and flat) is the first visual sign of a good or failed season.
Figure 2: The expanded chart — Total Monthly Rain (orange) and Anomaly (green), 2001–2026.
  • Runs of green below zero through a whole summer are the meteorological-drought signal: 2002–03, 2005, 2012, 2015–16 and 2023–24 all show it.
  • The large positive spikes (Feb 2017, Jan 2021) end meteorological drought in one month; rivers, dams and boreholes take a season or more to follow.
  • Download the CSV to compute a 3- or 12-month running total yourself if you need an SPI-like index for the current season (the SPEI layers stop in 2021).
Figure 3: Rainfall Monitoring and Forecast, expanded — daily rainfall since 2020 (orange) with the 7-day forecast (green) at the same station.
  • Daily data show dry-spell length inside a season, which monthly totals hide: the 2023/24 summer has few and small events compared with 2020/21.
  • The forecast points at the right edge are the sub-seasonal outlook for the station; a flat green tail in November means a late onset.
Figure 4: E-flow Monitoring and Forecasting site card (CROC-A24J-ROOIB) — the hydrological-drought check. The preview shows modelled flow since 2001; the card names the reach and site.
  • When rainfall and vegetation indices agree on drought, this is the confirmation: flows sitting on or below the requirement line in Expand (see Environmental flows).

docs.title: Worked example — assessing the 2023/24 season in retrospect
docs.text:
1. Add The Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) and set the timeline to March 2024. Large areas of southern Zimbabwe and Limpopo Province sit below 35 — peak-season stress.
  2. Add Rainfall Anomalies, click the Ingwizi circle: the chart (Figure 1) shows Nov 2023–Feb 2024 all orange — a failed season. Figure 3's SPI-12 has crossed −1.5 (severe).
  3. Add SMAP Root Zone Soil Moisture (L4, Daily) for February 2024 — the root zone confirms the rainfall deficit reached the crop.
  4. Add Eflow Alert Levels: dry-season 2024 sites on the Shashe, Mzingwane and Sand rivers show Level 4–5.
  5. Add Drought Risk – Agriculture (6-month): risk concentrates where the stressed VCI overlaps communal farming areas. That map, captured as a Story, is the briefing.
  6. Add Limpopo Rainfall Anomaly Forecast for the next season (2024/25): a wet anomaly — and Figure 2 confirms 2025 came in well above the mean, with the Beit Bridge flood of February 2025 (see Floods).

docs.title: Briefing checklist
docs.text:
• Current VCI class over the main cropping areas, with month and year
  • Rainfall deficit: seasonal total vs mean, and SPI/SPEI value at 3 and 12 months
  • Root-zone soil moisture relative to the seasonal norm
  • E-flow alert levels and reservoir storage class per sub-basin
  • Sectoral risk classes (agriculture, water, food & nutrition) by district
  • Seasonal outlook and its confidence
  • Story link reproducing the scenes

docs.title: Limits to keep in mind
docs.text:
• SPEI hazard layers cover 2010–2021 — a climatology baseline, not a live index. Use CHIRPS, the Rainfall Anomalies charts and the anomaly forecasts for the current season.
  • NDVI/VCI respond to any vegetation change (harvest, fire, land clearing), not only drought — cross-check with rainfall.
  • SMAP is coarse (the 1 km SMAP-Sentinel product is sharper but less frequent); it saturates in wetlands and irrigated fields.
  • Seasonal forecasts are probabilistic anomalies; read them as odds, not predictions.
  • Station charts (rainfall anomaly, e-flow) need a signed-in session.

docs.title: The question
docs.text:
An ecologist, a river-basin regulator or a dam operator needs to know whether each reach of the Limpopo is receiving the flow its ecosystem needs, where flows have fallen below alert levels, and how a change in releases or abstraction would alter the ecological risk.

Who Decision Cadence Environmental regulators (DWS, ZINWA, DNGRH, DWA) Enforce the Ecological Reserve / EWR; approve or refuse abstraction licences Monthly compliance review Dam operators Size and time environmental releases Weekly in the dry season Park and conservation agencies (SANParks, Gonarezhou, Limpopo NP) Trigger drought-response actions for aquatic biota On alert-level change LIMCOM e-flow task team Cross-border e-flow reporting under the Limpopo Watercourse Commission agreement Quarterly

At a glance

  • 31 monitored sites on 16 river reaches, each with a Recommended Ecological Category (mostly C; the estuary reach is D) and a risk region (RR1–RR10).
  • Alerts run from Level 1 (requirement met) to Level 5 (severe shortfall). The alert text states the top-up needed, e.g. "Add 2.709 m³/s to the river to maintain E-flows".
  • Crocodile (West) at Rooibokkraal: winter flows are 43–69 % below natural (abstraction), summer flows are near-natural; compliance 98.6–99.7 % of days per year since 2015.
  • Limpopo, Shashe–Mzingwane reach: mean monthly flow 102 m³/s, peaks up to 2,575 m³/s; monthly deficits occur almost every dry season.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. Explore data → search E-flow → add E-flow Monitoring and Forecasting. Sites appear along the river network, labelled by river code (e.g. LIMP-A71L-MAPUN, CROC-A24J-ROOIB).
  2. Add Eflow Alert Levels on top. The colour tells you the current class; start with the worst (dark red = Level 5).
  3. Click a site. The chart opens with four series — SWAT Present Flow, E-Flow (the requirement), Availability Surplus and Deficit. Hover any point to read values; drag across the chart or pick start and end dates to zoom to a season. Figures 1–2 below explain what you are looking at.
  4. Add SWAT Incremental Contributions to understand why: a deficit at a downstream site with healthy upstream contributions points to abstraction or storage in between, rather than a dry catchment.
  5. Add SWAT and Observed Sites and compare modelled flow with the nearest gauge in the chart — this is how much to trust the model at that reach.
  6. Scenario testing. Open the SWAT Extraction Tool (bottom-right icon). Choose the Flow Type (Natural Flows or Present Flows), enter the Channel ID shown in the site's feature info (e.g. cha0978 for the Crocodile site), set the Start / End Date, and FETCH DATA. Use the MAP tab to confirm the channel, TABLE for the numbers, and PROBFLO to see the ecological risk category the flow implies.
  7. Add Aquatic Ecoregions (LIMIS) and the Suitability layers to weigh a deficit by the sensitivity of the reach; add MiniSASS Sites to see whether citizen-science river-health scores agree.
  8. Capture the alert map and the chart as a Story for the e-flow committee.

docs.text:
The figures below are the portal's own charts, captured from the Feature Information panel (click a feature) and from the Charts dock that opens with the panel's Expand button. Every station, dam and site chart in the portal follows the same pattern: a summary card, a preview chart, Expand to enlarge, Download for the CSV.

Figure 1: E-flow Monitoring and Forecasting — the site card for CROC-A24J-ROOIB (Crocodile West at Rooibokkraal) with the modelled-flow preview since 2001, Show Raw Data, Advanced Chart, Expand and Download.
  • The card names the river code (used by the API and the SWAT Extraction Tool), the reach description and the site; the preview is present-day flow only.
  • Advanced Chart opens the analytics view (regime, compliance, deficit heat-map) for the site in the live portal.
Figure 2: The same site after Expand — four series: SWAT Present Flow, Natural Flow, Availability Surplus and E-Flow (the requirement), 2001–2026, m³/s.
  • The E-Flow requirement (green) is the low, seasonal line at the bottom; present flow (pink) rides above it in most months. Where pink dips to the green line in winter, the reach is at Level 2–3.
  • Wet-season peaks (300–560 m³/s in 2004, 2014, 2017, 2021, 2025) are near natural — this reach is altered in the dry season, not the wet.
  • Drag across a winter to zoom: the gap between pink and green in m³/s is the deficit the alert message asks the dam operator to release.
Figure 3: The Limpopo main stem, Shashe to Mzingwane (LIMP-A71L-MAPUN), expanded. Peaks reach 2,500 m³/s (2021) while the requirement stays below ~120 m³/s.
  • On a main-stem site the wet-season peaks dwarf everything else; zoom into the dry months to see the deficits, or read the Deficit series in Show Raw Data.
  • Compare with Figure 2: the same requirement logic, an order of magnitude more water.
Figure 4: The SWAT channel card for cha0978 — the Crocodile channel that feeds the e-flow site. Its Channel ID is what you type into the SWAT Extraction Tool (Flow Type, Start/End Date, FETCH DATA → MAP / TABLE / PROBFLO).
  • Channel geometry (stream order 4, 3.58 million ha drained) tells you how much upstream catchment — and abstraction — sits behind the site.

docs.title: Alert levels and what to do
docs.text:
Alert level Meaning Typical action Level 1 Present flow ≥ requirement None; record compliance Level 2 Present flow within ~10 % below the requirement Notify abstractors; review releases Level 3 Moderate shortfall Curtail non-essential abstraction on the reach Level 4 Large shortfall; forecast worsening Environmental release from upstream storage; restrict irrigation Level 5 Severe shortfall (flow near zero) Emergency release; suspend licences; monitor biota (fish kills, water quality)

The alert message states the top-up in m³/s — the number to hand to the dam operator.

docs.title: Worked example — attributing a winter deficit
docs.text:
1. In August, Eflow Alert Levels shows the Crocodile (West) site CROC-A24J-ROOIB at Level 3.
  2. Click the site: SWAT Present Flow is ~0.8 m³/s against an E-Flow of 2.1 m³/s (Figure 1, August) — a deficit of ~1.3 m³/s.
  3. Add SWAT Incremental Contributions: the upstream sub-catchments still contribute a few m³/s, so the catchment is not dry.
  4. Add SWAT and Observed Sites; the nearest gauge confirms the low flow — the model is trustworthy here.
  5. Open the SWAT Extraction Tool, Flow Type Natural Flows, Channel cha0978, June–September of the current year: natural August flow is ~2.6 m³/s. The shortfall is abstraction and storage, not climate.
  6. PROBFLO tab: at 0.8 m³/s the reach sits in a high ecological-risk band; at 2.1 m³/s it drops to moderate. That difference — 1.3 m³/s for eight weeks — is the release request.

docs.title: Compliance-report checklist
docs.text:
• Alert level per site (map captured as a Story scene)
  • For each site at Level 3+: present flow, requirement, deficit (m³/s) and spell length
  • Attribution: catchment contribution vs abstraction / storage
  • Gauge agreement with the model
  • Scenario tested in the SWAT Extraction Tool and PROBFLO risk before/after
  • Recommended release or licence action, with volume and duration

docs.title: Limits to keep in mind
docs.text:
• All flows here are SWAT model outputs, calibrated against gauges. Where the nearest gauge disagrees with the model, weight the gauge.
  • E-flow requirements are themselves the product of an assessment method; the PROBFLO risk categories are probabilistic, not thresholds of harm.
  • Monthly series smooth over daily extremes — a month that is compliant on average can contain a week of zero flow.
  • Site charts and the SWAT Extraction Tool call the IWMI data API and require a signed-in session.

docs.title: The question
docs.text:
A disaster-management officer, a dam operator or a basin authority needs three answers as an event develops: is a flood coming, where will the rivers peak, and who and what is exposed — and afterwards, how does this event compare with the past.

Who Decision When they look National / provincial disaster management (INGD, NDMC, DCP, CPU) Pre-position teams, issue warnings, open shelters Daily in the wet season (Nov–Mar), hourly during an event Dam operators (Massingir, Loskop, De Hoop…) Pre-release or hold storage ahead of forecast inflow Each GloFAS model run (daily, 00:00 UTC) LIMCOM and national hydrology services Cross-border notification (Botswana → Zimbabwe/South Africa → Mozambique) On any High or Extreme reporting point Humanitarian and insurance analysts Size the affected population and assets Post-event, within days

At a glance — the basin on 13 September 2026

  • 876 forecast points are classified daily: 378 Normal, 252 Elevated, 187 High, 59 Extreme.
  • Limpopo at Beit Bridge (A7H004): alert level Normal, 24.6 m³/s forecast for the next 24 h; the station's flood thresholds are p90 = 131, p95 = 254 and p99 = 527 m³/s.
  • Benchmark events in the 1979–2026 record at Beit Bridge: February 2000 (7,070 m³/s, a ~1-in-49-year peak), January 2013 (5,095 m³/s) and February 2025 (5,060 m³/s).

docs.title: Before the event — outlook (lead time 3–30 days)
docs.text:
1. Explore data → Accumulated Precipitation (10-day) → Add to the map, then add Precipitation Prob. > 150 mm (10-day). Large probabilities over the upper catchments (eastern Botswana, the Gauteng–Limpopo headwaters, the Zimbabwe highveld) mean the lower basin should prepare — travel time from Beit Bridge to Chókwè is on the order of a week.
  2. Add Flood Summary Days 1–3, then 4–10, and toggle between them with the Workbench switches: the flood signal should propagate downstream as lead time grows. If it does not, the rain is forecast to fall on dry soils and empty channels and may be absorbed.
  3. Add Reporting Points (% Exceedance) and click a point on the map. The Feature Information panel gives the exceedance probability; use Show Raw Data for the numbers.

docs.title: During the event — observe and confirm (lead time 0–3 days)
docs.text:
1. Add GPM IMERG Precipitation Rate (Daily) and MODIS NRT Flood (1-Day). Where rain fell yesterday and standing water appears today, the forecast is verifying. An empty IMERG layer means no rain, not missing data.
  2. Add GloFAS Discharge Forecast – Verified Gauges and click the gauge nearest the community of concern — for the main stem use A7H004 Limpopo River @ Beit Bridge, A5H006 (Botswana border) or the Olifants gauges B7H015 / B7H026 in Kruger. The chart shows forecast discharge for each lead time against the station's own thresholds (see the chart below).
  3. Expand the gauge's card in the Workbench and lower the opacity of the flood layers to ~60 % so the basemap stays readable underneath.

docs.title: Exposure
docs.text:
1. Add Population and Settlements (LIMIS) beneath the flood layers (drag to reorder in the Workbench). Use Compare with 100-year Flood Hazard (Climatology) on one side and the forecast footprint on the other to see whether the event is within or beyond the design baseline.
  2. For the Lower Limpopo (Chókwè–Xai-Xai) add the 20 / 50-Year Flood Lines – Lower Limpopo (LIMIS); anything forecast beyond the 50-year line is exceptional and justifies evacuation planning.

docs.title: After the event
docs.text:
1. Add Rapid Flood Mapping (1 km extent) and Rapid Impact Assessment, and compare the mapped extent with MODIS Flood Frequency (2001–2024) and the Year 2000 Flood Inundation Boundaries (LIMIS) to rank the event historically.
  2. Capture the key scenes as a Story (one per phase: outlook, event, exposure, aftermath) and Share / Print for the situation report.

docs.title: Reading the charts
docs.text:
The figures below are the portal's own charts, captured from the Feature Information panel (click a feature) and from the Charts dock that opens with the panel's Expand button. Every station, dam and site chart in the portal follows the same pattern: a summary card, a preview chart, Expand to enlarge, Download for the CSV.

Figure 1: Feature Information for gauge A7H004, Limpopo River at Beit Bridge (GloFAS Discharge Forecast – Verified Gauges). The card gives the 24 h, 72 h and 30-day forecasts, the flow status, the linked SWAT channel and the model run; the preview chart shows the current year.
  • Read the three numbers first: 24.6 → 34.4 → 24.0 m³/s means a small rise this week, then recession — Moderate status, no alert. In the wet season the same card can read 500 → 1,500 → 900.
  • Model run is the date to quote in a situation report; Linked SWAT (cha0215) is the channel to open in the SWAT Extraction Tool.
  • The preview chart shows this year's daily flow: the two peaks near 1,500 m³/s (February and late March 2026) are the wet-season pulses that shape the annual maxima history.
Figure 2: The same gauge after Expand — the Charts dock with the full GloFAS record since 1979. Each colour is a forecast lead time; the orange series is the reanalysis.
  • The dock shows every archived forecast and the reanalysis on one axis: the 2000 (≈7,000 m³/s), 2013 and 2025 (≈5,000 m³/s) floods stand out immediately.
  • Hover a point to read the value and date; drag to zoom into a season; Download gives the CSV with one column per lead time.
  • Compare the current year's forecast spikes (right edge) against those historical peaks to judge severity — a forecast of 2,500 m³/s at Beit Bridge is a top-ten event.
Figure 3: The same template for a SWAT channel (GloFAS Discharge Forecast – SWAT Channels), here cha0978 on the Crocodile. Channel geometry (stream order, drained area, width, depth) helps judge whether a forecast discharge will overtop the banks.
  • Channel points fill the gaps between gauges: 1,436 channels versus 363 gauges. A channel 8.6 m deep and 696 m wide carries 19 m³/s without notice; a first-order tributary would not.
  • 30D forecast 2.4 m³/s against 19 m³/s today shows the dry-season recession — the forecast is for the flow to fall.
Figure 4: Rainfall Monitoring and Forecast station card (s20592s27943e, channel cha0036, upper Shashe): last 7 and 30 days, wet days, 7-day forecast and last rain, with the daily rainfall preview.
  • This is the trigger layer for the flood workflow: when 7-day forecast jumps to tens of millimetres over headwater channels, open the GloFAS points downstream.
  • Expand shows daily rainfall since 2020 with the forecast in green — the wet-season clusters (Dec–Feb) are where flood peaks originate.

docs.title: Worked example — a dry-season check (September 2026)
docs.text:
1. Open GloFAS Discharge Forecast – Verified Gauges, click A7H004 near Beit Bridge. The chart shows ~10–35 m³/s for the coming month — an order of magnitude below p90 (131 m³/s). Normal.
  2. Switch on Reporting Points (% Exceedance). A cluster of Extreme points sits on the Elefantes/Singuédzi below Massingir and on the Steelpoort. Click one: the Elefantes channels read ~45 m³/s against a p99 of ~39 m³/s. That is Massingir releasing water, not a storm — the dam is at 90 % and drawing down for irrigation (see Reservoir monitoring).
  3. Add GPM IMERG Precipitation Rate (Daily): blank. No rain fell yesterday, which confirms the reading.
  4. Nothing to escalate; capture the view as a Story scene titled "Baseline — dry season" so that wet-season scenes can be compared against it.

docs.title: Situation-report checklist
docs.text:
• Date/time of the GloFAS model run quoted (shown on the gauge chart)
  • Rainfall outlook: 10-day totals and probability over each headwater region
  • Reaches forecast High / Extreme, with lead time and peak estimate
  • Observed confirmation (IMERG yesterday, NRT flood today)
  • Exposed settlements and population inside the forecast footprint
  • Reservoir status upstream (storage %, likely releases)
  • Comparison with 2000 / 2013 / 2025 benchmark events
  • Share link to the Story reproducing the map

docs.title: Limits to keep in mind
docs.text:
• IMERG shows nothing on dry days — an empty layer is not a broken layer. It is also near-real-time with a lag; check the date in the timeline.
  • NRT flood detection from MODIS/VIIRS is daily, optical, and misses water under cloud and vegetation; use it to confirm, not to rule out.
  • GloFAS is a global model downscaled to basin channels; verified gauges are the anchor — trust channel forecasts more where a gauge agrees. Thresholds are statistical (percentiles of the station's own record), not surveyed flood levels.
  • The flow-status classes are relative: Extreme at a small channel can be a few m³/s. Always read the discharge value.
  • Several LIMIS layers are historical snapshots (e.g. the 2000 flood); they do not update.

docs.title: The question
docs.text:
A water-resources planner or scheme manager wants to know where irrigated land is, whether it is growing, and how much water it consumes over a season — without waiting for licence returns or field surveys.

Who Decision Cadence Catchment / water management agencies (DWS, ARA-Sul, ZINWA, WUC) Licence compliance, detection of unregistered irrigation, allocation caps Seasonal (post-harvest) Irrigation boards and scheme managers Quota use, scheduling, efficiency benchmarks between blocks Monthly in season Dam operators Release planning against downstream irrigation demand Weekly (dry season) LIMCOM / water-accounting analysts Sectoral consumption for the basin account Annual

At a glance

  • Irrigated Mapping classifies irrigated cropland at 20 m from Sentinel-2, as a time series — the layer to watch for expansion.
  • Major schemes (designed → currently irrigated): Lower Limpopo 70,000 → 45,000 ha, Chókwè 30,000 → 22,000 ha, Loskop 27,000 → 19,000 ha, Tuli Block 15,000 → 12,000 ha, Groot Letaba 10,000 → 8,000 ha.
  • Managed (irrigated) land is 2 % of the basin but ~8 % of its evapotranspiration; its ET peaks in February and stays at 15–20 % of peak through the rainless winter — water that must come from dams, rivers and boreholes.
  • Loskop Dam, which supplies the largest South African scheme, has averaged 96 % full since 2017; its one supply crisis was 2016 (42 %).

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. Explore data → Search the catalogue → Irrigated Mapping → Add to the map. The layer is time-varying, so a timeline appears beneath the map.
  2. Use Ideal Zoom on the Workbench card to frame the layer, then use the timeline arrows to step between dates. Irrigated fields stand out as sharp, regular shapes (centre-pivot circles in the Tuli Block and Loskop; canal blocks at Chókwè) that stay green through the dry season.
  3. Add Irrigation Areas (LIMIS) and compare: irrigation detected outside the registered schemes is a first signal of unlicensed or expanding use. Along the Limpopo main stem between Botswana and South Africa, riverside pivots outside the LIMIS polygons are common.
  4. Add Blue ET Africa. In the Workbench, lower its opacity to ~60% so the fields remain visible underneath. Bright blue-ET over a field means it is drawing on irrigation water, not rain.
  5. Use Compare (Map Tools) to put Blue ET on the left and Green ET on the right for the same month — in August the contrast is starkest: green ET is near zero everywhere, blue ET marks every irrigated block.
  6. To quantify a scheme: open Water Use Time-series (Irrigated Areas) (Polygon) from Water Use Monitoring and Analysis, select or draw the area of interest (or the LIMIS scheme polygon) and run it. The result is a monthly time series of water use in m³ for that polygon that you can read directly or download.
  7. Add Beneficial Fraction Africa over the same scheme: blocks with high blue ET but a low beneficial fraction are losing water to bare-soil evaporation — candidates for scheduling or mulching advice.
  8. Add Dams & Reservoirs Basin Level Estimates and click the supplying dam (Loskop, Tzaneen, Middle Letaba, Massingir/Macarretane) to check whether the season's demand can be met (Figure 3).
  9. Story → Capture Scene for the before/after dates, and Share / Print the link.

docs.title: Worked example — sizing a scheme's seasonal use
docs.text:
1. Add Irrigation Areas (LIMIS) and zoom to the Loskop Irrigation Scheme on the Olifants below Loskop Dam.
  2. Add Irrigated Mapping; step the timeline from an early to a recent year. Compare irrigated pixels inside and outside the LIMIS boundary — pivots along the Olifants downstream of the scheme are the growth.
  3. Run Water Use Time-series (Irrigated Areas) (Polygon) on the scheme boundary for the last two hydrological years. Read the monthly m³; sum Oct–Sep for the seasonal total and note the winter share (Figure 2's shape).
  4. Add Blue ET Africa and Beneficial Fraction Africa for February: the blocks with high blue ET and low beneficial fraction are the ones to visit.
  5. Click Loskop in Dams & Reservoirs Basin Level Estimates: 104 % on 10 September 2026, forecast still above 90 % in November — the coming season's allocation is secure. Repeat for Middle Letaba (10.5 %): that scheme's 2,500 ha cannot be fully supplied this season.
  6. Capture the scheme map, the water-use chart and both dams as a Story.

docs.text:

docs.title: Limits to keep in mind
docs.text:
• Satellite ET products are modelled estimates at their native resolution (WaPOR downscaled, Africa-wide ET layers); use them for patterns and trends, and validate volumes against metered abstractions where they exist.
  • Irrigated Mapping is classified from imagery; cloud cover in the wet season can reduce confidence for individual dates — look at several. Irrigated pasture and orchards under netting can be under-detected.
  • The polygon Water Use Time-series runs a server-side process; large areas take longer, and it needs a signed-in session. It returns consumption (ET), not abstraction — conveyance losses are extra.
  • Scheme metadata (command area, irrigated area) are compiled from national sources and gazettes; treat them as indicative.

docs.title: The question
docs.text:
A dam operator, a bulk-water utility or LIMCOM staff want to know how full the basin's reservoirs are, how each has trended through the season, and what inflows the coming weeks are likely to bring — including for dams with no telemetry, by watching them from space.

Who Decision Cadence Dam operators and national water authorities (DWS, ZINWA, ARA-Sul, WUC) Release schedules, irrigation quotas, spill preparedness Weekly Bulk-water and municipal utilities Restriction levels, alternative sources Monthly; weekly below 30 % Irrigation boards Seasonal allocation (typically set in Oct) Seasonal LIMCOM Basin-wide storage reporting, drought / flood coordination Monthly

At a glance — 14 September 2026

  • 231 dams with storage estimates (445 dams in the layer); 84 % full basin-wide (7,107 of 8,454 Mm³).
  • By country: Botswana 90 % (10 dams) · Mozambique 91 % (4) · South Africa 82 % (147) · Zimbabwe 75 % (70).
  • Status: 128 Full, 25 Adequate, 20 Low, 56 Critical / Empty — the critical ones are mostly small farm dams, but Middle Letaba (180 Mm³) stood at 10.5 % in July 2026.
  • Outlook: the ensemble forecast has basin storage falling ~15 points to ~70 % by 30 November 2026 before the rains.
  • Massingir (2,260 Mm³, the largest) is at 90 %; Loskop at 104 %; De Hoop at 120 % (over full supply).

docs.title: How storage is estimated
docs.text:
Each dam in Basin Level Estimates carries a method and a confidence tier; read them in the feature-info panel before quoting a number.

Confidence Method Typical error High (Tier 1) Gauged level or satellite altimetry with a dam-specific area–capacity curve (Massingir: R² 0.997, MAPE 1.8 %) ± a few % Medium (Tier 2) Truncated-cone geometry, or capacity fraction with known dam height ± 10 % Low (Tier 3) Capacity-fraction / empirical power law from surface area alone ± 20 % or more No data No storage model (214 of the 445 dams) —

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. Explore data → search Reservoir → add Dams & Reservoirs Basin Level Estimates, then Dams and Reservoirs (LIMIS) for names. Use Ideal Zoom. Symbol colour is the status class.
  2. Click a dam. The Feature Information panel gives current %, volume, capacity, method, confidence and the storage chart with forecast (Figure 1). Use Show Raw Data or the CSV download for the table.
  3. Add Reservoir Levels – Water Area Timeseries and click the same reservoir: the chart shows water-surface area through time. A shrinking area through the dry season and recovery after rains is the normal cycle (Figure 3); a multi-year decline is the concern.
  4. For a long-term view, add Reservoir Levels – Yearly Aggregated by Channel and compare years side by side.
  5. See it. Add Rolling Monthly GeoMAD (Sentinel-2) and step the timeline to two dates a year apart; use Compare (left/right) to watch the shoreline move. Add Water Observations – All-Time Frequency to see the full-supply footprint the reservoir should fill.
  6. Inflows. Add Streamflow Gauging Stations (LIMIS) and GloFAS Discharge Forecast – SWAT Channels; click the channel upstream of the dam for the forecast hydrograph. Rising forecast inflow against a low reservoir is good news; against a full one it is a spill risk (see Floods).
  7. Capture a scene per reservoir as a Story for the operations meeting.

docs.text:
The figures below are the portal's own charts, captured from the Feature Information panel (click a feature) and from the Charts dock that opens with the panel's Expand button. Every station, dam and site chart in the portal follows the same pattern: a summary card, a preview chart, Expand to enlarge, Download for the CSV.

Figure 1: Dams & Reservoirs Basin Level Estimates — the Massingir card: current level 90.2 %, latest estimated volume 2,038 Mm³, status Full, capacity 2,260 Mm³, dam height, reservoir area, catchment, year built, mean and min/max volume, the estimation model (altimetry_level) and its R² (0.9974), with the storage preview.
  • Model and R² are the confidence check: altimetry_level with R² 0.997 is Tier 1; a capacity_fraction dam with no R² is a Tier 3 estimate (± 20 %).
  • Min / max 83.9 – 2,485 Mm³ frames the history: the dam has been effectively empty (2003, 2005) and above full supply (2008).
  • Expand ▾ offers four series — Estimated Volume, Observed Volume, % Capacity, Area; Download this Table gives the CSV.
Figure 2: Massingir after Expand → Estimated Volume: volume (Mm³, left axis) and % of capacity (second axis) since 2002, with the observed points overlaid.
  • Where the estimate (blue) and observations (orange) coincide the model is calibrated; the straight segments (2010–13, 2016–19) are gaps with no observations — read them as trend only.
  • The annual saw-tooth since 2021 is the operating cycle: fill to 100–105 % in March, draw down to ~65–75 % by November for Chókwè irrigation.
Figure 3: Reservoir Levels – Water Area Timeseries for Massingir Dam, expanded: satellite water area (ha, blue) with observed volume (Mm³) and observed capacity fraction where a gauge record exists.
  • The water-area series continues after the gauge record ends (2019) — this is how the portal monitors dams with no telemetry: area from satellite, converted to volume by the calibrated curve.
  • Area and volume move together but not proportionally (a flat reservoir loses area quickly at low levels); that non-linearity is the area–capacity curve the Tier 1 model encodes.
Figure 4: Loskop Dam (Olifants), Expand → Estimated Volume, 2016–2026 (Mm³ and %).
  • Three drawdowns stand out: 2016 (to ~150 Mm³, 42 %), 2019 (~250 Mm³) and late 2024 (~250 Mm³) — each the end of a dry season before the summer refill.
  • The flat top at ~350–365 Mm³ is full supply; values above it are spill periods. This is the chart to read against the seasonal band in the collapsed section below.

docs.title: Worked example — a September operations review
docs.text:
1. Add Dams & Reservoirs Basin Level Estimates. Sort by eye: most large dams are Full; Middle Letaba is red.
  2. Click Middle Letaba (Vhembe): 10.5 % on 5 July 2026, 18.9 of 180 Mm³, method ml_isotonic, Medium confidence. The storage chart shows a multi-year decline. Click Reservoir Levels – Water Area Timeseries on the same dam — the satellite area confirms the shrinkage, independent of the model.
  3. Add Streamflow Gauging Stations (LIMIS) and GloFAS Discharge Forecast – SWAT Channels; the Middle Letaba inflow channel forecasts negligible flow for 30 days. No relief before the rains: the Middle Letaba scheme's allocation must be cut (see Irrigation water use).

  5. Click De Hoop: 120 % — above full supply, so any early-season storm on the Steelpoort spills straight through. Flag for the flood watch.

docs.title: Operations-report checklist
docs.text:
• Basin, country and sub-basin storage % with the "as of" date
  • Dams Low / Critical, with method and confidence
  • Dams above full supply, with inflow forecast
  • Each key dam's position relative to its seasonal band
  • Forecast storage at 30 November (median and dry scenario)
  • Recommended quota, restriction or pre-release actions
  • Story link

docs.title: Limits to keep in mind
docs.text:
• Satellite water-area series are optical: cloud gaps in the wet season and narrow, tree-lined arms of a reservoir reduce accuracy.
  • Area does not capture depth; a shallow reservoir can look full while holding little — this is why Low-confidence dams carry ± 20 % error.
  • Level estimates and forecasts are modelled where telemetry is absent — they replace nothing where a gauge exists. Readings above 100 % are real (water above full-supply level) but short-lived.
  • The estimate date varies by dam (some are weeks old); always quote current_date from the feature info.
  • Storage and forecast charts require a signed-in session.

docs.title: The question
docs.text:
A basin planner or LIMCOM analyst needs a consistent balance of the basin's water: how much arrives as rain, how much leaves as evaporation and transpiration, how much runs off, how much is consumed by each sector, and how that balance is changing — the evidence base for allocation between the four riparian countries.

The portal follows the Water Accounting Plus (WA+) framework: a resource-base sheet (inflows, storage change, landscape ET, utilisable outflow) with ET split by four land-use classes — Protected, Utilized, Modified and Managed.

Who Decision Cadence LIMCOM secretariat and Technical Task Team Basin-wide allocation, transboundary reporting Annual accounts; hydrological-year review (Oct–Sep) National planners (DWS, DWA, ZINWA, DNGRH) Reconciliation strategies, licensing caps Annual Irrigation and hydropower sectors Efficiency targets, water-productivity benchmarks Seasonal Researchers and donors Track change and intervention impact Multi-year

At a glance — WA+ accounts 2003–2024

  • Rainfall 265 km³/yr on average → ET 249 km³/yr (94 %) → outflow to the sea 6.8 km³/yr (2.6 %).
  • Range: rainfall from 151 km³ (2015) to 511 km³ (2021); outflow from 0.4 km³ (2005) to 52 km³ (2021).
  • 2024: rainfall 196 km³ against ET 278 km³ — the landscape drew 80 km³ from storage.
  • Land use: Utilized 76.6 % of area, Protected 15.6 %, Modified 5.9 %, Managed water use 2.0 % (8,038 km²).
  • Managed land use consumes ~8 % of basin ET — the only share that can be reallocated.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. Frame the balance. Explore data → add CHIRPS Historical Rainfall and Evaporation Africa. Set the timeline to the same month on both. Rain in, evaporation out: where evaporation exceeds rainfall the landscape is drawing down storage (Figure 1 shows this at basin scale for 2024).
  2. Split consumption. Replace Evaporation with Blue ET Africa and Green ET Africa, using Compare side by side. Blue ET is water that had to be supplied — the managed part of the balance; Green ET is rain used in place.
  3. Judge productivity. Add Beneficial Fraction Africa. High consumption with a low beneficial fraction is water lost without benefit — the first place to look for savings.
  4. Follow the runoff. Add SWAT Incremental Contributions and Mean Annual Runoff (LIMIS): which sub-catchments generate the river, and how does modelled contribution compare with the long-term mean. Add Water Yield by Zone (LIMIS) and Water Requirements by Zone (LIMIS) to see where demand exceeds yield.
  5. Attribute sectors. Add Irrigation Areas (LIMIS) and Hydropower Evaporation Footprint (Africa); for a scheme-level number, run Water Use Time-series (Irrigated Areas) (Polygon) over the scheme boundary.
  6. Account for transfers and storage. Add Inter-basin Water Transfers (LIMIS), Transmission Losses (LIMIS) and Dams & Reservoirs Basin Level Estimates — water that moves across the boundary, is lost in transit or sits in storage closes the balance.
  7. Check against stations. Add Water Balance Stations (LIMIS) and Evaporation Stations (LIMIS); click a station for observed values to validate the satellite terms.
  8. Open the WA+ Dashboard. Add Limpopo Basin Water Balance (WA+ Dashboard) and click the basin marker: the compiled accounts open as a Sankey (resource-base sheet) with a downloadable CSV of every term by month since 2003.
  9. Save the assembled view as a Story, one scene per term of the balance.

The figures below are the portal's own charts, captured from the Feature Information panel (click a feature) and from the Charts dock that opens with the panel's Expand button. Every station, dam and site chart in the portal follows the same pattern: a summary card, a preview chart, Expand to enlarge, Download for the CSV.

Figure 1: Limpopo Basin Water Balance (WA+ Dashboard) — the basin marker's card, with Show Raw Data, Advanced Chart and Balance Dashboard buttons. The Balance Dashboard opens the compiled WA+ accounts (resource-base sheet as a Sankey) in the live portal.
  • This single marker is the entry point to the accounts: Balance Dashboard for the sheets, Download for the monthly CSV of every term since 2003.
Figure 2: The WA+ site after Expand — every term of the monthly balance (some 35 series: inflows, ET by land-use class, outflows, storage change) on one axis, 2003–2021.
  • The dock plots all terms at once, which is only useful for spotting the seasonal rhythm: the pink rainfall inflow peaks each summer; the yellow/orange ET terms follow one to two months later.
  • Turn series off in the legend to isolate a term — e.g. keep Inflow Precipitation Rainfall and Outflow ET Landscape Utilized to see that in dry summers ET exceeds rain.
  • For analysis use Download (one column per term) or the Balance Dashboard; the collapsed section below shows what the annual totals look like.
Figure 3: SWAT and Observed Sites — the card for gauge A2H012FW (Krokodil at Kalkheuwel): status, latest discharge (16.55 m³/s on 2 Sep 2026) and an Advanced Chart button. Gauges like this are the ground truth the accounts are validated against.
  • Observed discharge at the basin's gauges is the outflow term measured, not modelled; where it disagrees with the WA+ outflow, the account needs adjusting.
